  6. Report to Police（Minutes 25-30): Call 110 or go to the nearest police station to file a report and get a receipt. You'll need this receipt for insurance claims and bank disputes.

Scenario 2: Scammed — The 72-Hour Golden Response Period

After discovering you've been scammed, the most important thing is to stay calm. Panic-driven decisions can lead to secondary losses. Follow these steps:

  1. Immediately Stop All Transfers: No matter what the scammer says, don't transfer another cent. "Transfer another deposit and we'll return your previous money" is a classic secondary scam tactic.
  2. Preserve All Evidence: Don't delete chat history! Don't delete call logs! Screenshot chat records, transfer records, and the scammer's account information. These are critical evidence for reporting and recovering funds.
  3. Immediately Call 96110: This is the national anti-fraud hotline (96110). The operator will guide you through emergency payment interception — if the transfer was recent (usually within 24 hours), the bank may be able to freeze the recipient's account and intercept the funds.
  4. Call 110 to Report: Take your phone, ID card, and transfer receipts to the nearest police station to make a statement.
  5. Contact Bank / Payment Platform: Inform them of the fraud and request freezing of the involved accounts. If your credit card was fraudulently used, request the bank to initiate a chargeback.
  6. Change All Passwords: On another secure device, change passwords for your Apple ID / brand account, WeChat, Alipay, and bank apps, and enable two-factor authentication.

Scenario 3: Phone Infected with Virus/Trojan — What to Do?

If your phone shows these symptoms — random pop-up ads, auto-installing strange apps, sudden phone bill spikes, abnormal data consumption — it's likely infected with malware:

  • Step 1: Enter Safe Mode— On Android, long-press the power button to turn off, then long-press to turn on. After the startup vibration, press and hold the volume down button until you enter Safe Mode ("Safe Mode" appears in the bottom left corner). In Safe Mode, all third-party apps are disabled, making troubleshooting easier.
  • Step 2: Uninstall Suspicious Apps— In Safe Mode, go to Settings > App Management, sort by time, and uninstall any recently installed apps you don't recognize.
  • Step 3: Install a Security App and Scan— Download "Tencent Mobile Manager" or "360 Mobile Safe" and run a full scan.
  • Step 4: Factory Reset（Ultimate solution) — If the above methods don't work, back up important data and then factory reset. Note: factory reset will delete all data — back up photos, contacts, and other important files first.
  • iPhones Rarely Get Viruses— iOS's sandbox mechanism makes it very difficult for malware to survive. If your iPhone acts abnormally, it's most likely a bug or settings issue in an app, not a virus. Factory reset solves 99% of problems.

Scenario 4: Account Hacked — Quickly Regain Control

  1. Change Password Immediately: If you can still log in, change your password immediately. The new password must be completely different from the old one.
  2. Kick Out Other Devices: In account security settings, find "Login Device Management" and kick all unrecognized devices offline.
  3. Check Login History: Review login records from the past 7 days. If there are logins from unfamiliar locations, your account has indeed been hacked.
  4. : This feature can help you locate, lock, play sound, and even remotely wipe all data after your phone is lost. It's the last line of defense. Many people skip this step when buying a phone, and when they want to use it later, they find it wasn't enabled—and it's too late.: If you haven't enabled two-factor authentication, do it right now. This is the most effective way to prevent your account from being hacked again.
  5. Check Bound Information: Check whether the phone number and email bound to your account have been changed. If they have, use the account appeal function to recover it.
  6. Check Payment Settings: If WeChat or Alipay was hacked, check whether password-free payment and auto-deduction settings have been tampered with, and whether bank cards have been added to unfamiliar accounts.

Scenario 5: Receive Extortion Messages — Don't Panic, Don't Pay

Common extortion tactics come in two forms: ① "I have your compromising videos/photos, pay up or I'll send them to everyone in your contacts"; ② "Your phone has been hacked, pay or I'll lock it." When encountering this:

  • 99.9% Is a Scam: They don't actually have any of your private data. They mass-send the same extortion message to tens of thousands of people — some people will always get scared and pay.
  • Don't Reply, Don't Pay: Replying tells them "this number is active," marking you as an "extortable target" — leading to more harassment.
  • Screenshot and Save Evidence: Then block the sender.
  • Change Passwords: If worried, change passwords for your main accounts for peace of mind.
  • If There's a Real Privacy Leak Risk: Report to police. They have experience handling these cases.

Scenario 6: AI Deepfake / AI Voice Cloning Scams — Seeing Is No Longer Believing

Since 2024, AI deepfake and voice cloning technology has enabled scammers to "become" your family, boss, or friends in video calls. "Mom, I'm in trouble, transfer money quick" — the person in the video looks and sounds exactly like your son, but it's actually fake. This is one of the hardest-to-detect and most dangerous scam tactics today.

Step 1: Spot the Flaws — Four Common AI Forgery Telltale Signs

  • Abnormal Blink Frequency: Real people blink 15-20 times per minute. AI deepfakes often blink too rarely or with stiff rhythm.
  • Lip Sync Misalignment: Look closely — there's a fraction-of-a-second delay between lip movements and the audio you hear.
  • Blurred Facial Edges: The face outline, near the ears, and hair edges tend to have "frayed edges" or flickering.
  • Inconsistent Lighting Direction: Highlights and shadows on the face don't match the background lighting direction, or facial features don't "turn" correctly in profile view.

Step 2: Three Ways to Verify Identity

  • Ask Them to Perform Specific Actions: Ask the other person toturn their head, cover their face, or put a hand over their mouthand then open and close their mouth. AI deepfakes are most likely to "fail" during occlusion and large-angle head turns — the face will distort or lag behind movements.
  • Ask Questions Only They Would Know: Make up a fake question, like "Which hospital did we take our dog to last time?" — a scammer won't know the answer or will stammer.
  • Call Back a Known Number: Hang up the video call and directly call back using the number saved in your contacts. Scammers can't control real phone numbers — calling back exposes them immediately.

Step 3: Reporting Process After Confirming Fraud

  1. Immediately Stop Transfers: No matter how "urgent" it seems, pause first. Anyone who pushes you to "transfer quickly, don't hang up" is almost certainly a scammer.
  2. Preserve All Evidence: Screen-record and screenshot the video call, chat records, the scammer's account, and transfer receipts — these are key materials for technical forensics.
  3. Call the 96110 Anti-Fraud Hotline: Tell them it's an "AI deepfake/voice cloning" scam — the operator will initiate emergency payment interception.
  4. Call 110 to Report: Bring all evidence to the police station to make a statement, specifically noting that AI forgery technology was used, to help police classify the case.
  5. Set a SIM card PIN: Scammers may use your forged video to scam others — post a warning in your social media or family group chat in advance.

Scenario 7: SIM Swap Attack (SIM Hijacking) — Your Number Was "Stolen"

This is an attack many people haven't heard of, but it's extremely dangerous.SIM swap (SIM card hijacking)refers to an attacker forging your identity information and impersonating you at a carrier store to get a replacement SIM card. Once successful, your phone's signal suddenly disappears, while the attacker's phone — with the new SIM card — receives all your SMS verification codes. Alipay, banks, WeChat — all gates are wide open.

How to Detect It? Three Warning Signs of SIM Swap

  • Phone suddenly shows"No Service" / "No SIM Card", but you haven't touched the SIM card, and restarting doesn't help — this is often the moment of hijacking.
  • Receiving a "card replacement successful" or "business processing successful" text from your carrier — but you didn't request it.
  • Suddenly unable to receive verification codes, but can't receive other texts either — because SMS has been hijacked to the attacker's SIM.

Protection Measures — "Lock" Your SIM Card Too

  • Set a SIM Card PIN: Path: Settings > Phone > SIM PIN. Once enabled, you must enter the PIN every time the phone restarts or the SIM is moved to a different phone. Even if an attacker gets the card, they can't use it.
  • Enable Carrier Secondary Verification: Log into the China Mobile / China Unicom / China Telecom app, find "Security Center" or "Business Processing Verification," and enableNon-owner card replacement SMS alertsverbBusiness processing secondary password verification. This way, when someone tries to replace your card, the store clerk will require additional identity verification.
  • Don't Rely Solely on SMS Verification for Important Accounts: For high-value accounts like banks and Apple ID, prioritize usingauthenticator apps（Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator) orhardware keysrather than SMS verification codes.
  • Watermark ID Card Copies: On copies needed for business transactions, write "For XX use only" — attackers often impersonate you using leaked ID information.

Emergency Response After Hijacking — Speed Is Everything

  1. Immediately Call Carrier Customer Service to Report Loss: China Mobile 10086 / China Unicom 10010 / China Telecom 10000, request immediateservice suspension and freeze on card replacement, preventing the attacker from continuing to use your number.
  2. Log Into Key Accounts from Other Devices: Use a computer or family member's phone to immediately change passwords for banks, Alipay, WeChat, and Apple ID, and kick off unfamiliar devices.
  3. Freeze Payment Accounts: Alipay 95188 to report loss, WeChat Security Center to freeze, bank customer service to freeze online banking.
  4. Take Your ID to a Carrier Store: Personally bring your ID to a company-owned store to get a replacement SIM and restore your number.
  5. Report to Police: SIM swap constitutes the crime of "infringement of citizens' personal information." Bring all evidence (suspension time records, financial losses, card replacement records) to report to police.
  6. Comprehensive Review: After restoring your number, systematically check recent login records and financial transactions for signs of impersonation.

Prevention Beats Cure — 5 Daily Habits

  1. Lock screen password + two-factor authentication — enable both
  2. Confirm "Find My Phone" is enabled
  3. Set SIM card PIN (Settings > Phone > SIM PIN) — if phone is lost, others can't use your SIM
  4. Don't install apps from unknown sources, don't click unfamiliar links
  5. Regularly back up important data (photos, contacts, chat records)

Hands-On: Make Your Own "Emergency Contact Card"

  1. Find a piece of paper and write down these numbers: carrier customer service (China Mobile 10086 / China Unicom 10010 / China Telecom 10000), bank customer service, 96110 anti-fraud hotline, 110 police, family phone numbers.
  2. Write down your Apple ID / brand account registration email and backup contact methods.
  3. Keep this paper in your wallet or stick it on the fridge — don't store it in your phone, because when something happens, your phone might not be with you.
  4. Check right now: Is "Find My Phone" enabled? Is the SIM card PIN set?

Chapter Summary

  • Phone loss golden 30 minutes: borrow phone to call → remote lock → report SIM lost → freeze payments → notify family → report to police
  • After being scammed, 72 hours: stop transfers → preserve evidence → call 96110 → report to police → contact bank → change passwords
  • Phone virus: Safe Mode → uninstall suspicious apps → security scan → factory reset (ultimate solution)
  • Account hacked: change password → kick devices → check login history → enable 2FA → check bound info → check payment
  • Extortion messages are 99.9% scams — don't reply, don't pay, screenshot and block
  • AI deepfake/voice cloning scams: look for blink/lip sync/edge/lighting flaws — ask them to turn head and cover face, ask private questions, call back known number
  • SIM swap hijacking: be alert if phone suddenly shows "No Service" — set SIM PIN, enable carrier secondary verification, switch important accounts to authenticator apps
  • 5 daily prevention habits: lock screen + 2FA, Find My Phone, SIM PIN, don't install unknown apps, regular backup

VI. Outlook (Chapters 33-41)

Now that we've covered practical present-day tips and emergency plans, let's unleash our imagination and look at the storms brewing on the horizon. This chapter is short, but it points toward the big directions for the next 5-20 years — Will phones disappear? What will replace them? How will our relationship with the digital world be reshaped?

Chapter 33: Future Outlook — The Next Journey of Smartphones

Phones won't disappear overnight, but their "monopoly" may be eroded by a new generation of devices. This chapter covers three things: what next-gen devices look like, how the phone may "disappear" to become a new identity foundation, and the ethical issues we must consider ahead of time.

I. AR/VR and Spatial Computing: The "Second Desktop" Beyond Phones

The competition for next-gen devices has begun. The most likely candidates to divert time from phones are AR/VR and spatial computing devices:

  • Vision Pro Successor: The launch of Apple Vision Pro marked the official arrival of the "spatial computing" concept, but the first generation's price (starting at 29,999 yuan) and weight remain barriers. A lighter, cheaper Vision is expected in 2026-2027, bringing spatial computing from "developer toy" to "early majority." At that point, iPhone may become the computing companion and data hub for Vision glasses.
  • Another future evolution direction for phones may be "invisibility." It will transform into an omnipresent "behind-the-scenes promoter," becoming the sole cornerstone of your digital identity.: Open a "second desktop" in front of your eyes, making digital information as ubiquitous as air. Meta and Ray-Ban's smart glasses have sold millions of pairs, and domestic brands like Rokid, XREAL, and INMO are also releasing consumer AR glasses. By 2025-2026, AR glasses can do real-time translation, navigation HUD, and AI assistant conversations, but they're still limited by waveguide display and battery life — 3-5 years from "replacing phones."
  • Smart Rings and Wearables: Samsung Galaxy Ring, Oura Ring, and other smart rings are gaining popularity, serving as "body-worn sensors" that complement the phone's health monitoring. The phone's role is shifting from "all-in-one terminal" to "hub + multiple lightweight accessories."

II. Brain-Computer Interface: Thought as Interaction Medium

Thought itself will become an interaction medium, but this path is longer than imagined:

  • Neuralink Latest Progress: Musk's Neuralink completed its first human implant in 2024 — the first subject, Noland Arbaugh, controlled a computer mouse with his thoughts to play chess. Currently, implantable BCIs (brain-computer interfaces) primarily target assistive scenarios for paralyzed patients, aiming to help them "operate" the digital world again.
  • Non-invasive BCI: Multiple companies are developing non-invasive headbands (such as Kernel, OpenBCI) that can read brain signals without surgery, but with far lower precision than invasive ones. We're still quite far from "typing with thoughts."
  • Consumer Outlook: BCI is 10-20 years from consumer-level phone interaction, but may first be used in accessibility assistance and focus monitoring. Ethical and privacy issues ("Whose privacy do my brain waves belong to?") will become debate focal points before the technology matures.

III. The Phone's "Disappearance" and New Identity Foundation

Another future evolution direction for the phone may be "disappearing" — becoming an omnipresent "behind-the-scenes enabler" and the sole foundation of your digital identity:

  • : Your cloud personal data vault is the center.: Instantly complete "prove you are you" authentication — no need to manually enter verification codes when logging into any service.
  • An ultimate question always exists: Are we "gods" empowered by technology, or "brains in vats" fed by algorithms?: Pre-set digital asset inheritance plans during new device activation, making "digital afterlife" a factory default.
  • When you unconsciously light up the screen every few minutes, is this your habit or a designed "addictive behavior"?: Your cloud-based personal data vault is the center; hardware is just an access point. Change phones or devices — your identity and data always follow you.

IV. Ethical Reflection: Are We Still the Masters of Our Phones?

Let automation be your faithful "co-pilot."

  • AI Ethics: When on-device AI understands your preferences better than you do, is your "choice" an expression of free will or a guided outcome? When AI Agents place orders and reply to messages on your behalf, where do responsibility and boundaries lie?
  • Data Sovereignty: Does your health data, brain wave data, and biometric data belong to you, the device manufacturer, or the cloud service provider? The Personal Information Protection Law and EU GDPR are just starting points — the true implementation of "data portability rights" and "the right to be forgotten" still has a long way to go.
  • Digital Divide: AI phones, foldable screens, and satellite communications are widening the gap between those who "can afford" and those who "can't." Equitable access to digital infrastructure will become a new social issue — just as critical as "knowing how to use the internet" was 20 years ago.
  • Build your stable "digital rear base."
  • Regularly perform "digital decluttering" and "social fasting."

V. Stay Connected, Stay Independent — Your Digital Life Philosophy

No matter how technology evolves, these digital life philosophies will still apply 10 years from now:

  1. Try It: Draft Your "Personal Digital Device Terms of Service"
  2. Write a simple "terms of service" for you and your phone to define your relationship. For example:
  3. Article 1: My attention time belongs to me. You should proactively enter "Do Not Disturb" mode when I am working/spending time with family.
  4. Article 2: My personal data is my property. Your primary responsibility is secure encryption and convenient syncing.
  5. Article 3: Our common goal is to improve life efficiency and experience. If you make me addicted through manipulative design, I have the right to uninstall you.

V. Appendices

Write a simple "terms of service" for yourself and your phone (and future AR glasses and AI assistants) to define your relationship. For example:

  • Appendix A: New Phone Unboxing "Step-by-Step" Guide
  • 1. Unboxing Inspection "Three-Step Process":
  • Check Appearance

Chapter Summary

  • Vision Pro and AR glasses are new computing entry points beyond phones, but won't replace phones in the short term
  • BCI is 10-20 years from consumer use; ethical issues will mature before the technology does
  • The phone is evolving toward "disappearing" — from device-centric to identity-centric
  • AI ethics, data sovereignty, and the digital divide are core issues for the next 10 years
  • Staying connected while staying independent is the timeless philosophy of digital life

Chapter 34: In-Depth Guide to Car-Phone Connectivity — The Fusion of Phone and Automobile

Cars are evolving from "four wheels plus a sofa" to "four wheels plus a smartphone." Whether you drive a gas car or an EV, the relationship between your phone and car infotainment system determines your driving experience. This chapter clarifies the three routes for car-phone connectivity, the characteristics of each camp's system, and tips that make driving easier.

I. Three Routes for Car-Phone Connectivity

There are currently three approaches to connecting phones with cars. Understanding them means understanding the entire ecosystem:

  • Phone Casting to Car Screen: The car screen acts as just a "monitor" and "speaker" — computing and map data come from the phone. Representative solutions: Apple CarPlay, Google Android Auto, Huawei HiCar, Baidu CarLife. The advantage is that the phone ecosystem is directly brought to the car without reinstalling apps; the disadvantage is that the car's own hardware capabilities go unused.
  • Deep Integration of Phone and Car System: The car system is independent but shares accounts, apps, and data with the phone, and can even "hand off" tasks. Representative solutions: HarmonyOS Cockpit (AITO/Luxeed), BYD DiLink, NIO OS, Li Auto system. The advantage is an integrated experience; the disadvantage is being locked into one brand ecosystem.
  • CarPlay 2.0 Deep Integration: The next-generation CarPlay released by Apple in 2025 no longer just "casts" — it takes over core functions like the instrument cluster, climate control, and seat adjustment. Ferrari, Aston Martin, and Porsche are among the first to adopt it, marking a new era where "phone manufacturers drive the car infotainment system."

II. CarPlay / Android Auto / HiCar Comparison

The three mainstream casting solutions each have their strengths. Use this table when choosing a car or phone:

Solution Supported Phone OS Supported Car Models Feature Richness China Availability
Apple CarPlay iPhone only Very wide, most car models support it High — maps/music/phone/messages all work Good, works natively
Android Auto Android (domestic phones need service framework) Fairly wide, mainly joint venture/imported cars High, comparable to CarPlay Average, requires VPN to activate
Huawei HiCar Mainly Huawei phones, some support other Android Domestic cars and some joint venture models Fairly high, can integrate with HarmonyOS Cockpit Excellent, local ecosystem
Baidu CarLife Both iOS and Android Fairly wide, common retrofit for older cars Medium, updates are slow Excellent, local ecosystem

III. HarmonyOS Cockpit: Seamless Flow Between Phone and Car

If CarPlay is "casting phone to car," HarmonyOS Cockpit is "phone and car are already family." The collaboration between Huawei phones and AITO/Luxeed car systems represents the highest level of domestic car-phone connectivity:

  • Super Desktop: The car system directly accesses apps on the phone — no need to reinstall on the car. Music playing on the phone and navigation routes automatically continue on the car screen when you get in, and return to the phone when you get out — seamless throughout.
  • App Handoff: Navigation set on the phone is automatically taken over by the car system when you close the door; when you arrive at the parking lot, the phone continues walking navigation to the final destination. The "last mile" is no longer a gap.
  • Shared Account Between Phone and Car: Log into your Huawei account once, and the car system automatically syncs your music membership, map favorites, schedule, and contacts. The car and phone are different terminals of the same identity, not two independent systems.

IV. Car Systems from New Automakers

Domestic EV infotainment systems have evolved from "navigation + music" to mobile smart terminals, each with distinctive approaches:

  • NIO OS: The NOMI voice assistant is an industry benchmark — it can recognize multiple commands and contextual continuous dialogue, with emotional expressions. The NIO Phone turns the phone into a "car key + second screen," deeply integrated with the NIO ecosystem.
  • Li Auto System: Multi-screen interaction is the highlight — the front passenger screen can independently play shows, and the rear screen can play cartoons. "Task Master" lets you customize scenarios, like "auto-pause music when door opens, resume when closed."
  • Xiaomi HyperOS Car System: Deeply integrated with Xiaomi phones, watches, and home appliances. Alarms set on the phone remind you on the car system; when navigating home, the home AC turns on in advance. HyperOS connects the "person-car-home ecosystem."
  • BYD DiLink: The signature rotating screen — vertical for short videos, horizontal for maps, adapting to app orientation. Built-in app store leads in ecosystem richness among traditional automakers.

V. Phone as Car System — Can It Work?

If your car system is too old or too hard to use, can you just use your phone instead? The answer: yes, but it depends on the scenario.

  • Motorola Ready For / Desktop Mode: Some Motorola, Samsung, and Huawei phones support "Desktop Mode" — connect a monitor and it becomes a simple computer. In theory, it could connect to a car screen, but real-world compatibility varies, and it lacks car-specific interactions (like steering wheel buttons).
  • Phone Mount vs. Built-in Car System: If the built-in car system lags or maps are outdated, a sturdy phone mount + phone navigation is a practical choice. But note: ① small phone screen is hard to see while driving; ② summer heat can cause the phone to thermal-throttle or shut down; ③ long navigation drains battery fast — you need a car charger.
  • Recommendation: For short trips or temporary use, a phone mount is fine; for daily commuting and long trips, upgrading to a CarPlay/HiCar-enabled system or installing an aftermarket unit is better for both experience and safety.

Private repositories aren't absolutely secure either; sensitive information is best managed with environment variables, not in code repositories.

Regardless of which solution you use, operating your phone while driving violates traffic rules. A phone mount is only for "viewing navigation" — not for "operating the phone." Set destinations, switch songs, etc. only after pulling over, or use voice control.

VI. Practical Tips

  • Unstable Wireless CarPlay Connection: ① Turn off car Bluetooth and re-pair; ② Delete paired device records on the car side and reconnect; ③ Check if your phone is connected to multiple Bluetooth devices causing conflicts; ④ Update car firmware and phone system to the latest version; ⑤ If all else fails, switch to wired CarPlay — more stable.
  • Car Data Plan Used Up: ① Turn on phone hotspot and connect the car system to it; ② In car settings, switch "high data consumption" apps (like video and streaming music) to Wi-Fi; ③ Regularly clear the car's offline map cache.
  • Driving Mode Auto-Trigger: ① iOS "Focus" set to "auto-enable when connected to car Bluetooth," automatically blocking non-urgent notifications; ② Android "Driving Mode" or third-party apps (like Tasker) can auto-mute and auto-reply to messages when connected to Bluetooth; ③ Huawei phones can set "smart payment" to auto-switch music to the car system when you get in.

Tips When Choosing a Car

If you care about the infotainment experience, be sure to test at the dealership: ① Bring your phone and test CarPlay/HiCar connection stability; ② Test voice assistant response speed and command recognition; ③ Check if the app store has your frequently used apps; ④ Pay attention to OTA update frequency — good car systems are built through software iteration.

Hands-On: Optimize Your Car Connectivity Experience

  1. Confirm which connectivity solution your phone and car support (CarPlay / HiCar / Android Auto / CarLife).
  2. Clear the car's Bluetooth pairing list once, keeping only your commonly used phones to reduce connection conflicts.
  3. Set up a "Driving Focus" that auto-activates when connected to car Bluetooth.
  4. Download the car brand app (e.g., HarmonyOS Smart Driving, Li Auto, NIO App) to see if you can remotely control AC and check vehicle status.

Chapter Summary

  • Three connectivity routes: casting (CarPlay etc.), deep integration (HarmonyOS Cockpit etc.), CarPlay 2.0 deep integration
  • CarPlay has the widest ecosystem; HiCar has the best domestic experience; Android Auto requires workarounds in China; CarLife suits older cars
  • HarmonyOS Cockpit's Super Desktop, App Handoff, and shared accounts represent the deep integration direction
  • NIO NOMI, Li Auto multi-screen, Xiaomi person-car-home, BYD rotating screen — each has its own style
  • Using a phone as car system is only suitable for temporary scenarios — upgrade or install aftermarket for long-term use
  • Practical tips: CarPlay reconnection, phone hotspot for data, Bluetooth-triggered driving mode

Children and Phones Special Topic (Chapter 35)

The relationship between children and phones is one of the biggest headaches for this generation of parents. Give it too early, fear addiction; too late, fear falling behind. Control too much, fear rebellion; too little, fear losing control. This chapter doesn't take sides or lecture — it breaks down "when to give, how to manage, how to teach, how to protect" into actionable steps, helping you be a confident parent in the digital age.

Chapter 35: Children and Phones — An Educational Guide for the Digital Age

This chapter doesn't paint phones as "monsters," nor does it advocate "the earlier the smarter." We'll go step by step by age: giving devices, setting rules, teaching literacy, and protecting health.

I. At What Age Should Kids Get a Phone?

There's no standard answer, but there are age baselines. Giving a phone too early — the child's prefrontal cortex isn't fully developed, so self-control can't keep up with algorithms' "temptation design." Too late — the child may become "socially disconnected" from peers. Here are age-based recommendations:

  • Ages 3-6: Try to avoid phones entirely. If needed, no more than 15 minutes per session, with parent-selected educational cartoons, and must beco-viewed with a parent. Screen time has the greatest impact on vision and attention development at this stage.
  • Ages 7-9: Can "borrow" a parent's device for online classes, audiobooks, and research. Start establishing "request before use, return after" rules. No dedicated phone.
  • Ages 10-12: Consider a "feature phone" or kids' smartwatch for school commute communication. If a smartphone is truly needed, enable strict parental controls.
  • Ages 13+: Entering middle school, social needs increase. A smartphone can be given, but with a "usage agreement" and regular reviews.

The "Good Enough" Principle

A child's first phone doesn't need to be a flagship. "Excess performance" processors often end up running games. Choose a mid-range phone with adequate battery, eye-friendly screen, or an official refurbished model — easier to manage. Budget reference: 1,500-2,500 yuan covers most students' needs.

Smartwatch as a Transition

If you just want to solve the "can I reach them after school" problem, a kids' smartwatch is better than a phone. It can only make calls, send voice messages, and track location — no browser or short videos, naturally limiting "addiction gateways":

  • XiaoTianCai (Little Genius) Phone Watch: Most complete ecosystem, peer social "tap to add friend" is its core selling point, but the proprietary app ecosystem is relatively closed.
  • Huawei Kids' Watch: Good integration with Huawei phones, accurate positioning, supports video calls, high value for money.
  • Xiaomi Kids' Watch: Affordable, complete basic features, suitable for budget-conscious families.

When buying a watch, note: choose one that supports4G full network compatibilitymodels (2G/3G are being phased out), and check carrier kids' plan rates.

II. Complete Parental Control Guide

Before giving the device to the child, the first thing isn't turning it on — it's setting up parental controls. Both platforms have native solutions:

iOS: Screen Time
  • App Limits: Settings > Screen Time > App Limits — set daily time limits per app category (e.g., games 30 minutes).
  • Downtime: Set a daily "lights out" period (e.g., 22:00-7:00) — all apps gray out, only phone calls available.
  • Content Restrictions: Filter movies, web content, and app installs by age, and disable in-app purchases.
  • Family Sharing: Use the parent's iPhone to remotely manage the child's device, approve download requests, and view usage reports.
Android: Google Family Link / Brand Parental Controls
  • Google Family Link: Google's official solution — remotely manage device usage time, lock devices, view activity reports. Availability on domestic Android varies by model.
  • Xiaomi Kids Space: Settings > Kids Space — set usage time, whitelist apps, requires parent password to exit.
  • Huawei Student Mode: Settings > Healthy Phone Usage > Student Mode — restrict usage times and apps, supports remote management.
  • OPPO/vivo Kids Mode: Enable in "Settings" or the dedicated "Kids Space" app — similar principle.
Feature iOS Screen Time Android Family Link / Brand Solutions
App LimitsSupported, by categorySupported, per app
DowntimeSupportedSupported (brand solutions vary slightly)
Content FilteringSystem-level, more thoroughDepends on brand, varies
Remote ManagementFamily SharingFamily Link / Brand Cloud
App Install ApprovalRequires parent approvalFamily Link supports it

Parental Controls Aren't "Once and Done"

Kids can always find ways to bypass them (search "how to crack Screen Time" online — tons of tutorials). Technical measures are just the baseline — the real defense is parent-child communication and trust. I recommend reviewing usage reports together with your child monthly, rather than unilaterally monitoring.

III. Youth Mode

Major content platforms have built-in "Youth Mode" — when enabled, it limits usage time, filters inappropriate content, and disables in-app purchases and tipping. This is a legally mandated feature, butparents must actively enable it and set a password(Background).

  • Douyin/Kuaishou Youth Mode: 40 minutes daily (disabled 22:00-6:00), only curated science and educational videos shown — no livestreaming, no tipping, no recharging.
  • WeChat Youth Mode: Limits WeChat Pay (requires parent-authorized amount), restricts Official Account and Channels content, Shake and Nearby features are disabled by default.
  • Game Anti-Addiction System: National-level real-name authentication + time limits. Minors can only log into games on Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and public holidays from 20:00-21:00, for 1 hour per day.

Don't Use Parents' IDs for Real-Name Authentication to "Borrow Accounts"

Many kids use parents' IDs to register game accounts and bypass anti-addiction. This violates user agreements and removes protections. Parents should safeguard their payment passwords and identity information — don't "lend accounts" to children for convenience.

IV. Digital Literacy Education

Technology can block 90% of risks — the remaining 10% depends on the child's judgment. Rather than "no internet," it's more important to teach them "how to use the internet":

  • Privacy protection: Don't share real name, school, or home address with strangers. Don't send personal photos, ID cards, or family group photos. Keep location services off by default, only enable when needed.
  • Cyberbullying Recognition and Response: Being insulted, ostracized, or having photos maliciously edited are all forms of bullying. Tell your child: don't retaliate, don't delete evidence, tell a parent immediately. On WeChat, long-press the message to report — the platform will handle the bully's account.
  • Content Criticism: Teach children to distinguish "facts" from "opinions," recognize clickbait and sensationalism. Understand that algorithms only push what you want to see, not the whole picture. Treat "too good to be true" ads as always fake.
  • Cybersecurity: Don't click unfamiliar links, don't scan QR codes from unknown sources, don't download apps from non-official stores. Don't share passwords with anyone (including "best friends"). Anyone asking for verification codes is a scammer.

Hands-On: Sign a "Phone Usage Agreement" with Your Child

Writing rules down, both parties signing, and posting them prominently is far more effective than verbal agreements. Recommended contents:

  • Usage times: e.g., "Available 19:30-20:30 after homework is done."
  • No-phone zones: at the dinner table, in the bedroom before sleep, in class — phone put away.
  • Content boundaries: don't install apps without telling parents, don't private chat with strangers.
  • Violation consequences: e.g., "One violation halves next day's usage time."
  • Parent commitment: don't "scroll" on the phone in front of the child beyond agreed time — lead by example.

V. Healthy Usage Habits

Children's eyes, neck, and sleep are still developing — phone damage is greater than for adults:

  • Screen Time Recommendations: Ages 3-6: no more than 1 hour daily; ages 6-12: no limit for educational content, no more than 1 hour for entertainment; ages 12+: negotiate with the child, but entertainment no more than 2 hours.
  • Eye Protection Habits: Follow the "20-20-20 rule" — every 20 minutes of screen time, look at something 20 feet (about 6 meters) away for 20 seconds. No phone 1 hour before bed — blue light suppresses melatonin and affects sleep.
  • Posture Management: Keep the phone screen at eye level, don't hunch over. Get up and move after every 30 minutes of continuous use.
  • Family Shared Rules: Set "no-phone zones" at the dining table, bedroom, and study. During family movie time and outdoor activities, everyone puts their phone away — making "putting down the phone" a family culture, not a punishment for the child.

Parents Are the Best "Firewall"

Research shows a strong positive correlation between parents' phone usage time and children's. Demanding that children stay off their phones while scrolling short videos until late at night yourself makes the rules ineffective. To change your child, start by putting down your own phone.

VI. Digital Legacy and Children

This section is easily overlooked but very important. Children's digital assets (accounts, photos, stored value, game items) also face inheritance and privacy issues:

  • Inheritance of Children's Digital Assets: When a child unfortunately passes away, the inheritance process for social accounts, game accounts, and cloud photos is the same as for adults — requires death certificate and proof of kinship. Parents should set up "legacy contacts" or "emergency contacts" for children's important accounts in advance (e.g., Apple Legacy Contact, WeChat account inheritance).
  • Digital Privacy of Minors: The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that processing personal information of minors under 14 requires guardian consent, with dedicated privacy rules. Parents should regularly review the privacy policies of apps their children use frequently, and turn off "personalized recommendations" and "data sharing" toggles.
  • Account Registration Recommendations: Accounts registered for children should use parent-controlled email/phone numbers for unified management during the minor stage; account transfer can be done when the child reaches adulthood.

The Other Side of "Children's Digital Legacy"

Children are being "recorded" from birth — growth photos posted by parents, videos from kindergarten, health data from smartwatches. Once uploaded, this data is hard to completely delete. Before posting, think: Will the child feel embarrassed by this photo in ten years? Respecting your child's digital identity starts with restraining from "sharenting."

Chapter Summary

  • There's no standard age to give a phone, but ages 3-6 should avoid it, and before 13 use a kids' watch or feature phone as transition
  • "Good enough": choose a budget phone, not a flagship — excess performance equals excess temptation
  • iOS Screen Time and Android Family Link/brand parental controls are two technical defense lines — use them together for better protection
  • Youth Mode and game anti-addiction are legally required, but parents must actively enable them and guard the passwords
  • Digital literacy is more important than technical blocking: teach kids to recognize bullying, protect privacy, and critically evaluate content
  • Healthy habits start with parents — when you put down your phone, your child will too
  • Children's digital legacy and privacy are emerging issues — set up "legacy contacts" and restrain from sharenting

Chapter 36: Phones and Smart Home — Making Your Home Smarter

Phones can do something increasingly important — act as the "remote control" for the entire home. From a light bulb to a smart plug to a door lock, smart home is transitioning from "geek toy" to "everyday setup." This chapter clarifies protocols, ecosystems, hubs, and starter kits, ending with a security checklist to prevent "smart" from backfiring.

I. Smart Home Protocols: Who You Choose Matters

Before buying smart devices, check which protocol they support — this determines whether your phone and ecosystem can "command" them. There are currently four mainstream protocols, each with its own characteristics:

  • Matter Protocol: Released in 2022 by the CSA (Connectivity Standards Alliance), backed by giants like Apple, Google, Amazon, and Samsung. Its goal is singular — make all brands of smart devices speak the same language. In 2023-2026 it's rapidly becoming the unified standard. Devices that support it can simultaneously connect to Apple HomeKit, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Mi Home — no longer locked into a single ecosystem.
  • Thread Protocol: Matter's underlying network "pipe." Low power, self-healing mesh (if one node goes down, signals automatically reroute), fast response, no lag. Buy devices with a Thread border router (like HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, Xiaomi Hub Gateway) for a noticeably more stable experience.
  • Wi-Fi: High bandwidth, can connect directly to router, but high power consumption and prone to channel congestion with many devices. Good for cameras and robot vacuums that need to transmit large amounts of data.
  • Bluetooth (BLE): Simple provisioning, power-efficient, but short range and no mesh networking. Good for door locks and temperature/humidity sensors — small data devices.
  • Zigbee: Veteran low-power mesh protocol, requires a dedicated gateway. Devices are cheap and stable, but cross-brand interoperability is poor. Being gradually replaced by Matter + Thread.

One-Sentence Principle

When buying smart devices in 2026, prioritize the "Matter over Thread" label — the most future-proof choice today. Old devices that only support Wi-Fi or Bluetooth don't need to be rushed to replacement — keep using them, and switch to Matter for new purchases.

II. Three Ecosystems Comparison

Protocol is the "language," ecosystem is the "circle." Even if everything supports Matter, you still need to choose one primary ecosystem for automation and voice control. The three mainstream ecosystems compared:

Ecosystem —Veteran of the Android Camp Weakness Target Users
Apple HomeKit Strongest privacy (mainly local processing), smooth integration with iPhone/Siri/Shortcuts Fewer and pricier devices, requires HomePod or Apple TV as hub All-Apple household, users who value privacy and experience
Mi Home (Xiaomi) Most diverse devices, best value, Xiao Ai is useful Relatively closed ecosystem, data mostly cloud-based, more ads Budget-conscious, entry-level users wanting one-stop whole-home setup
Huawei Smart Connection (HarmonyOS) Seamless flow with HarmonyOS phone/tablet/watch, rapidly growing device count Limited overseas device support, ecosystem still catching up Huawei phone users, those who value "Super Device" multi-device collaboration

Ecosystem Selection Advice

Choose ecosystem based on your phone: iPhone users should prioritize HomeKit, Huawei users should prioritize Smart Connection, other Android users find Mi Home easiest. With Matter protocol, devices from different ecosystems can also be controlled by the same phone — no need to "pick a side" all at once.

III. Phone as Smart Home Hub

In most entry-level scenarios, the phone is your "smart home hub" — control lights, AC, curtains, and security through apps, and build automation scenes that let your home "run itself":

  • Device Control: Open the HomeKit / Mi Home / Smart Life app to remotely or locally toggle lights, adjust color temperature, set AC temperature, open/close curtains, and view camera feeds.
  • Automation Scenes: Combine "condition → action" — three commonly used scenes:
    • Home Mode: Location = home + dark → turn on entry light + turn on AC + close curtains + lock door.
    • Away Mode: Last person leaves (location = away or door locks) → turn off lights + turn off AC + turn off outlets + activate cameras + arm.
    • Sleep Mode: Every night at 23:00 → turn off main lights + close curtains + AC to 26°C + turn on night light.
  • NFC Tap: Stick an NFC tag by the door — tap your phone to trigger the corresponding scene (one tap turns on entry light, another switches to sleep mode). iPhone uses "Shortcuts" automation, Android uses "Wallet" or manufacturer apps to write.

Try It: Build a "Home Mode"

In your phone's smart home app, create a new automation under "Automations": set trigger to "Arrive at location" (home), add actions "turn on entry light," "set AC to 26°C," "close curtains." Save, go out for a walk, and see if the lights turn on automatically when you return — the satisfaction of the first successful automation is more thrilling than ordering a new device.

IV. Starter Kit Recommendations

No need to buy everything at once. Start with these four items to cover 80% of daily needs:

  • Smart speakers: Xiao Ai (Mi Home ecosystem, high value) / HomePod mini (Apple ecosystem, doubles as Thread hub) / Alexa (wide overseas ecosystem).Note: The speaker determines your voice ecosystem — choose the ecosystem first, then buy the speaker.
  • Smart Bulbs: Yeelight (Mi Home/Matter, adjustable color temperature and brightness, affordable) / Philips Hue (great color, stable, but requires Hue bridge, pricier).Note: Confirm the bulb socket size (E27/B22) and whether you need color tuning before buying.
  • Smart Plugs: Xiaomi Smart Plug (affordable, power monitoring) / TP-Link Kasa (good Matter support overseas).Note: When using with high-power appliances (water heaters, space heaters), check the rated power — don't overload.
  • Smart Door Locks: Lockin / Xiaomi (value for money, Mi Home integration) / Kaadas (traditional lock manufacturer, solid mechanical construction).Note: Confirm Matter or ecosystem support, check battery life and emergency keyhole location.

Purchase Order Recommendation

Smart speaker first (to set the ecosystem) → then smart bulbs and plugs (low barrier, immediate feedback) → finally locks and cameras (involve safety, choose carefully). Add one category at a time — expand after getting familiar, to avoid "bought but don't know how to use."

V. Security Precautions

The more smart devices you have, the larger the attack surface. These four rules are the baseline — check each one:

  1. Change Default Passwords: Default passwords for cameras, routers, and locks are all publicly available online. The first thing to do after purchase is change them to "long and unique" strong passwords.
  2. Update Firmware Promptly: Firmware pushed by manufacturers often fixes security vulnerabilities. Enable "auto-update" in the app, or manually check at least monthly.
  3. Network Isolation: Put IoT devices on a separate Wi-Fi (or guest network) from your phone and computer's main network. If one device is compromised, it can't easily threaten your important data.
  4. Privacy protection: Enable "privacy zones" on cameras (e.g., don't film bedrooms or bathrooms), disable 24-hour cloud recording; don't leave camera feeds open to third-party apps when you're not home.

Avoid These Pitfalls

  • Don't use the lock's "remote unlock" feature for strangers — prioritize temporary codes that expire after use.
  • Don't point cameras directly at your bed or out the window — you're leaking your own privacy.
  • Don't buy cheap "white-label" unbranded devices — they rarely get firmware updates, essentially installing a backdoor in your home.

Chapter Summary

  • Matter + Thread is the unified direction for 2023-2026 — prioritize this label when buying new devices
  • Three ecosystems each have strengths: Apple for privacy/experience, Mi Home for value, Huawei for multi-device collaboration
  • Phone can be the hub — set up "Home/Away/Sleep" scenes, and the home runs itself
  • Starter four: smart speaker, bulbs, plugs, locks — add in this order
  • Change default passwords, update firmware, isolate networks, enable privacy masking — four security baselines you can't skip

Chapter 37: Phones and Wearables — Synergy on Your Wrist

Smartwatches and rings are no longer just "phone notification devices worn on the body" — they're the phone's extended senses: measuring heart rate, swiping for transit, opening doors, finding your phone. This chapter helps you figure out "whether to buy, what to buy, and how to connect."

I. Two Camps and Pairing Logic

The core of wearable devices isn't hardware specs, but "who it pairs with and what it can do."

  • Apple Watch: Only pairs with iPhone via the [Watch] app. After pairing, it's essentially iOS's second screen — permissions, notifications, and health data all route through the iPhone.
  • Wear OS / Manufacturer Watches（Huawei WATCH, Xiaomi, Samsung Galaxy Watch): Pair with Android via each manufacturer's app ([Huawei Health], [Wear OS], [Galaxy Wearable]); pairing with iPhone has severely limited functionality — this is the "compatibility trap" you must confirm before buying.
  • Smart Rings（Oura Ring, Galaxy Ring, domestic rings): No screen — relies on sensors + long battery life. Connects via Bluetooth to a dedicated app, then syncs with the phone's health platform. The value is in "imperceptible wearing" — sleep and heart rate data is more continuous than with watches.

II. Three Essential Sync Features

  1. Notifications and Reminders: In phone [Settings] > [Bluetooth] or the manufacturer's app, sync "message notifications" to the watch. Recommend syncing only important apps (phone, WeChat, calendar) — otherwise your wrist buzzes hundreds of times a day.
  2. Payment and Access Control: Apple Watch — add transit/bank cards in [Wallet] to tap and pay; Android watches can "copy" physical access/transit cards to the watch NFC. Note that watch payments usually have a small password-free limit — report loss on the phone immediately if lost.
  3. Health Data Sync: Heart rate, blood oxygen, and sleep data collected by the watch should "flow" to the phone's health platform (Apple Health, Huawei Health, Google Fit) — otherwise it's a data island. Check the "data sharing/sync" toggle in the watch app.

III. Battery Life and Privacy

  • Battery Life: Charging every 1-2 days is normal for watches. Turn off "all-day heart rate" and "raise to wake" to extend it. Smart rings typically last 7+ days because they have no screen.
  • Privacy: Health data is sensitive — confirm whether data is uploaded to the cloud. Apple Health data is end-to-end encrypted by default; some domestic apps upload by default — turn off "participate in data analysis" in [Privacy Settings].

Hands-On Exercise

Open your phone's watch/health app and complete three tasks: ① Turn off one watch notification you don't want; ② Link a frequently used card to the watch; ③ Check whether last night's sleep data has synced to the phone. After these three steps, your wearable is truly "connected" to your phone.

Chapter 38: Travel and Phones — eSIM, Data Plans, and Offline Maps

When traveling abroad, your phone is your most essential tool: navigation, translation, payment, ticket checking. But roaming fees, no signal, and unusable apps can turn a trip into a disaster. This chapter is your "24-hour pre-departure" checklist.

I. eSIM in Practice: More Elegant Than Swapping SIM Cards

eSIM is a "virtual SIM card" written into the phone — no physical card needed to connect to a carrier.

  • Support Status: iPhone XS and later all support eSIM; most Android flagships support it, but Chinese domestic versions are often stripped (some only support physical SIM). Check the specs page for "Screen refresh rate automatically adjusts based on content (1-120Hz)—smooth and power-efficient." before buying.
  • International eSIM Data Plans: Buy destination data packages via apps (like Airalo, Holafly, carrier international plans) — use immediately upon landing, no SIM swap needed.Note that these are typically data-only — no voice calls— emergency calls require a physical roaming SIM or Wi-Fi calling.
  • Operation: [Settings] > [Cellular] > [Add eSIM] > Scan the QR code from the carrier. Multiple eSIMs can be stored simultaneously and switched as needed.

II. The Offline Trio: Maps, Translation, Payment

Signal may drop, but your tools can't.

  • Offline Maps: Google Maps / Amap / OsmAnd all support downloading regional offline packages. Download destination city + surrounding area over Wi-Fi before departure — navigation and search work offline.
  • Offline Translation: Google Translate, Youdao, and Baidu Translate all support offline language packs.Download destination language packs in advance, otherwise the translation app stops working in remote mountainous areas with no signal.
  • Overseas Payment: UnionPay/Visa/Mastercard bound to mobile wallet for overseas card payments or NFC (note: enable "overseas transactions" toggle); local wallets (GrabPay in Southeast Asia, PayPay in Japan, Toss in Korea) — register on arrival for convenience; Alipay/WeChat Pay overseas only work at merchants with "blue-green logos" — don't count on them for everything.

III. International Data Plan Comparison

Solution : High-end professional production. The iPhone 15 Pro series supports shooting Apple ProRes video (up to 4K 60fps), but the ProRes RAW format currently requires an external recording device — phones do not yet support shooting it directly. Characteristics Suitable For
Carrier International Roaming Package No number change, can receive verification codes Expensive, needs advance activation Short-term business
International eSIM Data Package Cheap, works on arrival Data-only, no voice calls Most leisure travelers
Local Physical SIM Card Cheapest, has local number Need to swap SIM, registration hassle Long-term / multi-country
Phone Hotspot Sharing One SIM serves the whole family Drains battery, depends on one device Family travel

Hands-On Exercise

Pick a country you want to visit in the future and complete: ① Check if your phone supports eSIM; ② Download the country's major city offline map in your map app; ③ Download the country's language offline translation package. These three steps take less than 10 minutes but prevent 90% of "landing blind" situations.

Chapter 39: Phones and Health Management — Turning Numbers into Action

Your phone and watch collect massive amounts of health data every day, but most people only look at "step count rankings." This chapter teaches you to understand metrics, choose the right apps, and avoid data anxiety.

I. Understand Four Core Metrics

  • Heart Rate: Resting heart rate of 60-100 bpm is normal; persistent low or high readings, or abnormal spikes during exercise are worth noting. Watch-based optical heart rate may be inaccurate during intense exercise — use as trend reference, not diagnosis.
  • Blood Oxygen (SpO₂): Normal is 95%-100%. Watches measure "instantaneous values" — a single low reading isn't cause for panic, but chronically low readings should be checked by a doctor. Sleep apnea screening requires medical-grade equipment — watches are just indicators.
  • Sleep: Focus on the long-term trend of "total duration" + "deep sleep proportion," not on losing 20 minutes on a particular night. Watches estimate sleep stages based on body movement + heart rate — accuracy is limited.
  • Women's Health: Cycle tracking combined with basal body temperature (supported by some rings/watches) can predict ovulation. Note: these features are positioned as "reference," not reliable for contraception or conception.

II. The Three-Layer Structure of Health Apps

  1. Collection Layer: Watch/ring sensors.
  2. Aggregation Layer: Phone health platforms (Apple Health, Huawei Health, Google Fit, Samsung Health). This is the "data ledger" — all apps read and write here.
  3. Application Layer: Third-party apps (Keep, Bohe, Sleep Cycle) pull data from the aggregation layer for analysis.

Key Action: In [Settings] > [Privacy] > [Health], check the authorization scope for each app. Third-party apps should only read the data they need — a running app has no reason to read your sleep details.

III. Mental Health and Digital Detox

  • Screen Time: iOS [Settings] > [Screen Time], Android [Digital Wellbeing]. The key isn't "how long" but "which apps take the most time and make you feel bad afterward."
  • Mental Health Apps: Meditation apps (Chaoxi, Calm), mood tracking apps (Daylio) can be supplementary, but can't replace professional help — seek counseling for persistent low mood.
  • Beware of "Data Anxiety": Staring daily at minor fluctuations in sleep scores and HRV (heart rate variability) causes anxiety. Look at health data in "weekly/monthly trends," not "daily."

Hands-On Exercise

Open your phone's health platform and export or screenshot your steps and sleep from the past 7 days. Find a notably low metric and set a small actionable improvement for next week (e.g., "phone in living room after 11 PM"). Write down the metric and the action — data is only valuable when it becomes action.

Chapter 40: AI Short Video Creation — From One Sentence to a Complete Video

AI is lowering the barrier for "shooting a short video" from "knowing how to edit" to "knowing how to describe." This chapter focuses on AI creation workflows accessible to ordinary people, not LLM principles.

I. Creation Pipeline and Tool Positioning

A short video = script + visuals + voiceover + editing. AI can intervene at every step.

  • Script: ChatGPT, Doubao, Kimi help you write titles, voiceover scripts, and hooks (the first 3 seconds). Prompts should include "audience + style + word count + emotion."
  • Visuals: Image-to-video (Kling AI, Jimeng, Runway) turns an image or a description into a few seconds of motion — good for B-roll and transitions; digital humans (HeyGen, Guiji, Tencent Zhiying) generate "virtual person speaking" videos from scripts — good for voiceover-style content when you don't want to show your face.
  • Voiceover: CapCut "Text-to-Speech," ElevenLabs, ByteDance TTS. AI voiceovers are quite natural now, but emotional variation is still weaker than real humans.
  • Editing: CapCut (mobile first choice) — "Auto Cut," "Auto Captions," and "AI Keying" dramatically lower the barrier.

II. Hands-On: Make a 30-Second Voiceover with CapCut AI

  1. Use AI to write an 80-120 word voiceover script (about 30 seconds).
  2. CapCut [New Project] > Import background image or digital human footage > [Text] > [New Text] paste script.
  3. Select text > [Text-to-Speech] choose voice > Generate voiceover.
  4. [Subtitles] > [Auto Captions] auto-align.
  5. Add BGM (CapCut music library, mind copyright) > Export 1080P vertical.

Copyright Red Line: AI-generated visuals/music may involve training data copyright — confirm platform licensing terms before commercial use. Don't use real people's faces for digital humans. Don't directly clone celebrity voices for voiceovers.

III. Platform Rules and Removing the "AI Feel"

  • Platform Rules: Platforms (Douyin, WeChat Channels, YouTube Shorts) have labeling requirements for purely AI-generated content, and some throttle "low-quality AI batch accounts." Recommendation: AI assistance + real person/voice, mixed output.
  • Three Ways to Remove the "AI Feel": ① Use real person/footage hooks in the first 3 seconds; ② Add personal specific details to the script; ③ Make the editing rhythm less regular — AI defaults to an "ad-like" rhythm; manually add a few pauses for a more natural feel.

Hands-On Exercise

Use a one-sentence prompt to have AI write a 30-second voiceover script (any topic), and complete "script → voiceover → subtitles → export" in CapCut. The goal isn't a viral hit but running through the complete pipeline once. After finishing, review: which step did AI save you the most time? Which step do you still want to manually edit?

Chapter 41: Vertical Short Drama for Beginners — A Hook Every 3 Minutes

Vertical short dramas (1-3 minutes per episode, intense conflict, fast reversals) are a content format that exploded since 2024. This chapter gives ordinary people who want to enter the space a "terrain map."

I. Script Structure: Hook-Driven

Short dramas aren't "shortened TV shows" — they're "conflict-amplifying hook machines."

  • Single Episode Formula: 3-second strong hook (slap, secret exposed, identity reversal) → 30-second setup → 60-second escalation → cliffhanger ending forcing binge-watching.
  • (: Stereotyped, label-based ("bullied son-in-law," "hidden billionaire"). Short dramas don't pursue complexity — they pursue "audience understands in one glance, feels satisfied in one second."
  • Pacing: An emotional beat every 15-20 seconds — avoid flat pacing. Mark each "emotional turning point" when writing the script.

II. Shooting: Phones Are Good Enough, But With Limitations

  • Equipment: Flagship phone main camera (4K 30fps) + gimbal + lavalier mic is enough to start. In vertical shooting, leave a "safe zone" in the composition (subtitles and platform UI shouldn't cover the face).
  • Lighting: Short dramas are often shot indoors — one soft main light + one rim light improves quality more than upgrading your phone.
  • Acting: Short drama acting tends to be exaggerated and fast-paced. Shoot multiple takes per shot, and speed up in post with "jump cuts" to compress pauses.

III. Platform Policies and Monetization

  • Platforms: Douyin/Kuaishou/WeChat Channels short dramas, Hongguo, Dianzhong, and other mini-program drama platforms. Each platform has preferences and red lines for themes (CEO, revenge, comeback) — read the "creator guidelines" before submitting.
  • Registration: Domestic short dramas must be registered as "online micro-short dramas" (key dramas, regular dramas). Mini-program dramas need a registration number to run ads. This is a compliance baseline, not optional.
  • Monetization: Revenue sharing (platform pays per valid view), ad-driven monetization (pay to unlock subsequent episodes), brand customization. Beginners shouldn't start by burning money on ads — first validate content with organic traffic.

Risk Warning: The short drama track is fast-moving, fiercely competitive, and highly homogenized. Treat it as "practice + small-amount trial and error" — don't go all-in with your entire savings.

Hands-On Exercise

Pick a short drama you've watched and reverse-engineer its script: write down what the "3-second hook," "mid-episode escalation," and "ending cliffhanger" of Episode 1 are. Then watch how Episode 2's opening picks up the cliffhanger. This deconstruction exercise gets you closer to "understanding short dramas" than shooting 10 bad episodes.

First, the conclusion:

Foldable screens are no longer "novelty toys," but neither are they a mainstream form factor that "everyone should buy"

Appendix F: Foldable Phone Purchasing and Usage Special Topic

Currently, there are two mainstream categories:

Horizontal Folding (Book-style)

: When closed, it's the size of a regular phone; when opened, it's nearly square like a small tablet. Representatives: Huawei Mate X series, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold series, Xiaomi MIX Fold series, vivo X Fold series. Main selling point: "one phone = phone + tablet".Vertical Folding (Clamshell-style): When closed, it looks like a compact powder case; when opened, it's a normal-sized phone. Representatives: Huawei Pocket series, Samsung Galaxy Z Flip series, OPPO Find N Flip, Xiaomi MIX Flip. Main selling point: "compact portability + cover screen quick view".

Key advancements in 2024-2025: Hinge lifespan is generally rated at 500,000 folds (opening/closing 100 times daily lasts 13 years), UTG ultra-thin glass has replaced early plastic films, creases are visible to the naked eye but barely perceptible by touch, prices have dropped from the 10,000+ yuan range down to the 5,000-6,000 yuan range.

  • One-Sentence VerdictIf your current slab phone fully meets your needs and you have no pain point of "screen not being big enough," don't buy a foldable. It's a "nice-to-have" device, not a "must-have" device.
  • II. Who Should Buy a Foldable Phone?Based on real user feedback, these groups have a high probability of finding foldables "worth it":

Key advances in 2024-2026: hinge life generally rated at 500,000 folds (100 folds/day for 13 years), UTG ultra-thin glass replacing early plastic films, creases visible but barely felt by touch, prices dropping from the 10,000 yuan tier to 4,000-5,000 yuan.

: Frequently view PDFs, annotate documents, and read long articles on their phone. When unfolded, the ~7.5-inch inner screen lets you view A4 PDFs without zooming—a transformative experience.

Frequent Travelers / Business Users

: Don't want to carry a tablet but find phone screens too small. Horizontal foldables let you view PPTs, sign contracts, and compare emails side-by-side—significantly more efficient than a slab phone.

Creatives Who Love "Flex Mode"

  1. : Fold to 90° and place on a desk—upper screen for framing, lower screen for shutter (selfies/timelapse); upper screen video, lower screen notes; upper screen livestream, lower screen comments—a form factor slab phones simply cannot achieve.Female Users Who Want Portability + Big Screen
  2. : Vertical foldables fit into small bags when closed, unfold to normal phone size, and the cover screen can serve as a makeup mirror or notification viewer.These People Should NOT Buy One
  3. If you only use your phone for short videos, WeChat, and calling—foldables offer zero benefit and are heavier and thicker instead.If you have small hands or wrist tendonitis—horizontal foldables weigh 230g+ when unfolded, making single-handed use tiring.
  4. If you're on a tight budget and plan to keep a phone for 4+ years—foldables have lower resale value than slab phones, and repair costs are high.III. Buying Guide: Check These 6 Metrics

Don't get dazzled by the word "folding"—focus on these key points when shopping:

  • Hinge Type
  • : Waterdrop hinge (shallower crease, longer lifespan, currently mainstream) is better than U-type hinge (deeper crease, early solution). Ask sales staff or check reviews to confirm which type.
  • Inner Screen Material

: Must be UTG ultra-thin glass, not early plastic film. UTG feels close to glass; plastic film feels indented under fingernails and easily retains marks.

Crease Performance

  • : Go to a store and unfold it yourself. The 2025 qualified standard: almost invisible head-on with screen on, visible as a shallow groove under angled light, slight depression when finger runs across but not sharp.Cover Screen Size
  • : For horizontal foldables, the larger the outer screen the better (ideally 6.4"+) so it works as a normal phone when closed; for vertical foldables, larger is more practical (4"+ allows replying to messages and viewing navigation).Weight & Thickness
  • : Horizontal foldables at 230-260g unfolded is normal; under 230g is excellent. Closed thickness of 12-14mm; under 12mm is thin. Vertical foldables must fit comfortably in a shirt pocket when closed to qualify.: Go to a physical store and unfold it yourself. The 2026 acceptable standard is: almost invisible when screen is on, a shallow groove visible under angled light, slight depression when fingers pass over but not sharp.
  • : Focus on inner screen crack repair cost. Some brands offer free inner screen replacement once in the first year; others charge 2,000-4,000 yuan out-of-pocket. This is the biggest hidden cost of owning a foldable.In-Store Experience Checklist
  • Open and close it 10 times yourself—feel if the hinge damping is smooth and if there are any unusual sounds.Unfold it and look at the crease under angled light, then look at it head-on with the screen on.
  • Hold it single-handed in unfolded state for 30 seconds—feel if the weight is acceptable.Try Flex Mode: fold to 90°, place on desk, try taking photos and watching videos.

Ask clearly about the standalone inner screen repair price and warranty policy.

  1. IV. Unique Foldable Usage Tips
  2. After buying one, here are experiences you can't get with a slab phone:
  3. 1. Split-Screen & Multitasking
  4. When a horizontal foldable is unfolded, most systems support top/bottom or left/right split-screen. Typical scenarios: upper screen for online course video, lower screen for notes; left side WeChat, right side documents; upper screen map navigation, lower screen music. Much more practical than slab phone split-screens because the screen is large enough that neither half feels cramped.
  5. 2. Flex Mode (90° Fold)

This is the "killer feature" usage of foldables:

Selfies / Group Photos

: Place on desk folded to 90°, upper screen for framing, lower screen for shutter—no need to ask someone else to take the photo.

Timelapse / Night Shots

: Same stable placement on desk—saves you from needing a tripod.

Video Calls

  • : Frees both hands; the other person sees you from a more natural angle too.Watching Videos
  • : Use as a mini TV on a desk—especially practical on airplane/high-speed rail tray tables.Cover Screen Preview + Inner Screen Shooting
  • : When using the rear camera to shoot yourself, the cover screen displays the live preview for more accurate composition.3. Cover Screen Quick View
  • When a vertical foldable is closed, the cover screen can: show time/notifications/weather, reply to WeChat (voice-to-text or quick replies), tap transit cards, view navigation, act as a makeup mirror (using front camera). No need to unfold every time—saves power and effort.4. Desktop Mode
  • Some horizontal foldables (Huawei, Samsung) can switch to "Desktop Mode" when unfolded. After connecting an external display, keyboard, and mouse, it works like a basic PC—adequate for temporary document processing and email replies. Not a primary productivity tool, but great for emergencies.V. Maintenance Tips: Help Your Foldable Last Longer
The most delicate parts of a foldable are the inner screen and hinge. These habits can significantly extend its lifespan:

Don't Force Open/Close in Low Temperatures

: Below 0°C, UTG glass becomes brittle. Warm it in your pocket for a few minutes before opening/closing. This is something written in every official manual but nobody reads.

Avoid Nails/Hard Objects Touching the Inner Screen

: The inner screen has a protective layer but is softer than the outer screen. Operate with your fingertips, never poke with fingernails.

Check for Foreign Objects Before Closing

  • : A single grain of sand caught inside when closing could directly crush the inner screen. Glance over it before closing.Don't Apply Regular Tempered Glass Film
  • : The inner screen can only use official specialized film or UTG protective film. Regular tempered glass film affects folding and touch functionality. Recommend going to official after-sales for screen protector application.Keep Dust & Liquids Away from the Hinge
  • : Although most claim IPX8 water resistance, dust resistance ratings are generally low. Be careful at beaches, construction sites, etc.Apply Even Force When Opening/Closing
  • : Don't violently flick it open with one hand. Opening smoothly with both hands from the center is most stable.High-Risk Scenarios for Inner Screen Damage
  • Catching headphone/charging cable when closing—directly cracks the inner screen.Mixing with keys in a bag—outer screen fine, but keys press creases into the inner screen.
  • Immediately opening/closing when moving from cold outdoors to warm indoors in winter—temperature difference causes glass stress changes.After a year of use, feeling "the crease got deeper" and trying to peel off the factory film—peeling the film will damage the inner screen along with it.

VI. Foldable "Pitfalls" & Realistic Expectations

  • Before buying, keep these things in mind:
  • The Crease Will Always Be There
  • : 2025 technology cannot achieve "completely invisible"—only "almost invisible head-on with screen on". If you're a perfectionist who would stare at the crease uncomfortably every day, don't buy.
  • Heavier & Thicker

: Horizontal foldables weigh 230g+ when unfolded—more tiring for single-handed use than slab phones. Closed thickness of 12-14mm makes pockets bulge more.

Battery Life Is Generally Average

  • : Because space must accommodate the hinge mechanism, battery capacity is compressed. At the same price point, battery life typically falls short of slab phones.: 2026 technology can't achieve "completely crease-free" — only "almost invisible from the front when screen is on." If you're a perfectionist who'll be bothered by the crease daily, don't buy.
  • : After one year, the second-hand price is usually 50-60% of the new phone price—drops faster than slab phones.Expensive Repairs
  • : Inner screen assembly repair costs 2,000-4,000 yuan; hinge repair costs 500-1,500 yuan. Check warranty policies clearly before buying.Inconsistent App Adaptation
  • : Mainstream apps have adapted to large screens, but niche apps may just be "stretched/enlarged" with mediocre experience.A foldable is not a "better phone"—it's "a phone in a different form factor." Buy it because you need its unique form, not because it's "more advanced."

Conclusion: Stay Curious, Stay Clear-Headed

Congratulations on making it this far.

This book covers everything from phone hardware to software ecosystem, from daily settings to developer mode, from security protection to digital legacy. If it helped you solve one practical problem — even just learning to turn off an unnecessary permission or forming a backup habit — then these words weren't written in vain.

But more important than any specific technique are two things:

  • Stay Curious: Phones change every year, AI is changing, foldable screens are changing, satellite communication is changing. The operation steps you learn today may be outdated tomorrow, but the curiosity of "wanting to know why" never goes out of date. Asking one more question — "What does this permission do?" "Where is this data stored?" "Could this feature leak privacy?" — is more useful than memorizing a hundred operation steps.
  • Stay Clear-Headed: The phone is a tool, not a master. It's designed to capture your attention, occupy your time, and guide your consumption. Using it is your choice; being used by it is your loss of control. Periodically check your screen time, and think "Am I using my phone to get things done, or is my phone consuming me?" — this isn't melodrama, it's a survival instinct in the digital age.

Technology changes, but human needs don't — we need security, connection, and respect. The phone is just a medium. The real "phone class" isn't in a book — it's in the moment you unlock your screen every day.

One Last Exercise

Close this book, pick up your phone, and do one thing:Take 30 seconds to think: what three things in your phone would you "truly regret losing"?Then, make sure they're backed up. This book was worth it.
